# Disorders of the glans penis and foreskin

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Pediatrics > Pediatric urology > Disorders of the glans penis and foreskin*

[Original Article Link](/library/oi00sf)

---

## Summary

Common disorders of the <u>glans penis</u> and <u>foreskin</u> include <u>balanitis</u>, <u>balanoposthitis</u>, <u>phimosis</u>, and <u>paraphimosis</u>. <u>Balanitis</u> refers to inflammation of the <u>glans penis</u>, while <u>balanoposthitis</u> refers to inflammation of both the <u>glans penis</u> and the <u>foreskin</u>. Management focuses on optimizing genital hygiene and topical treatments based on the underlying etiology. <u>Phimosis</u> is a congenital or acquired constriction of the <u>foreskin</u> causing inability to <u>retract</u> the <u>foreskin</u>. <u>Physiologic phimosis</u> is common in younger men and resolves with time. <u>Pathologic phimosis</u> is treated with careful genital hygiene and <u>topical steroids</u>, but <u>circumcision</u> may be required. <u>Paraphimosis</u> is a urological emergency in which the <u>foreskin</u> is trapped behind the <u>glans penis</u> in uncircumcised or partially <u>circumcised</u> individuals, causing constriction of the <u>penis</u>. <u>Paraphimosis</u> needs to be manually reduced, but if unsuccessful, surgical management is required to avoid penile <u>necrosis</u>.

---

## Balanitis and balanoposthitis

### Definition [[1]](/library/_DW5Sn0)




* Balanitis: inflammation of the <u>glans penis</u>

* Posthitis: inflammation of the <u>foreskin</u>

* Balanoposthitis: inflammation of both the <u>glans penis</u> and the <u>foreskin</u>





### Etiology [[1]](/library/_DW5Sn0)[[2]](/library/7vW4Yn0)[[3]](/library/iDWJVn0)




* Infectious 

* <u>Candida</u> (e.g., candidal <u>balanitis</u>, <u>diaper dermatitis</u>)

* <u>Sexually transmitted infections</u> (e.g., <u>gonorrhea</u>, <u>chlamydia</u>, syphillis)

* <u>Human papillomavirus</u>

* <u>Herpes simplex virus</u>

* Inflammatory [[4]](/library/RDWlVn0)

* Irritant balanoposthitis: <u>balanoposthitis</u> due to irritation of the <u>skin</u> (e.g., excessive cleaning with soap)

* <u>Allergic reaction</u> (e.g., <u>contact dermatitis</u>, <u>fixed drug reaction</u>)

* Balanitis xerotica obliterans: <u>lichen sclerosus</u> of the <u>glans penis</u> and <u>foreskin</u>, characterized by pruritic, white <u>plaques</u> with <u>epidermal</u> <u>atrophy</u> and scarring

* <u>Lichen planus</u>

* <u>Psoriasis</u>

* Balanitis circinata: an inflammatory, ulcerating <u>balanitis</u> associated with <u>reactive arthritis</u>

* Zoon balanitis: an inflammatory <u>balanitis</u> that is commonly found in older, uncircumcised men and presents as an <u>erythematous</u> patch on the glans

* Premalignancy

* <u>Bowen disease</u>

* <u>Erythroplasia of Queyrat</u>





> [!TIP]
> Recurrent candidal <u>balanitis</u> may be caused by undiagnosed <u>diabetes</u>. [[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

### Clinical features [[1]](/library/_DW5Sn0)[[2]](/library/7vW4Yn0)[[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* <u>Pruritus</u>, <u>pain</u>, and <u>edema</u> of the <u>glans penis</u>

* <u>Erythema</u> of the glans and/or <u>foreskin</u> with possible <u>erosions</u> or ulcerative lesions

* Penile <u>exudate</u> and/or discharge

* Associated symptoms (e.g., <u>fever</u>, <u>arthralgias</u>, <u>malaise</u>, <u>lymphadenopathy</u>)





### Diagnostics [[2]](/library/7vW4Yn0)




* <u>Clinical diagnosis</u>

* Additional testing if etiology is uncertain, e.g.:

* <u>Subpreputial</u> swab and <u>KOH test</u> to confirm <u>candida</u> infection

* <u>Subpreputial</u> <u>Gram stain</u> and culture to confirm bacterial or <u>candida</u> infection

* <u>STI testing</u> (e.g., gonorrrhea, <u>chlamydia</u>, syphillis, <u>HSV</u>)

* <u>Biopsy</u> if there is a concern for premalignant lesions





### Management [[2]](/library/7vW4Yn0)




* Optimize hygiene, e.g., daily <u>foreskin</u> <u>retraction</u> and washing.

* Avoid known irritants (e.g., soap, perfumes); consider <u>emollients</u> as an alternative to soap.

* Provide disease-specific treatment such as <u>antibiotics</u> for bacterial infections, topical <u>antifungals</u> (e.g., <u>clotrimazole</u>) for mild <u>fungal infections</u>, and <u>topical steroids</u> for irritant or <u>allergic reactions</u>.

* Manage underlying conditions, e.g., <u>psoriasis</u>, <u>reactive arthritis</u>, <u>diabetes</u>, <u>lichen sclerosus</u>, <u>lichen planus</u>.

* Consult urology for persistent or recurrent episodes.  [[2]](/library/7vW4Yn0)





#### Disease-specific treatment




* Candidal infection

* Mild-to-moderate: topical <u>clotrimazole</u> DOSAGE for 7–14 days [[2]](/library/7vW4Yn0)

* Severe: oral <u>fluconazole</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[2]](/library/7vW4Yn0)

* Anaerobic bacterial infection: <u>metronidazole</u> DOSAGE for 1 week [[2]](/library/7vW4Yn0)

* Aerobic bacterial infection

* Mild-to-moderate: topical <u>mupirocin</u> DOSAGE for 7–10 days [[2]](/library/7vW4Yn0)

* Severe: systemic <u>antibiotics</u>, e.g., oral <u>cephalexin</u> DOSAGE for 7 days [[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* <u>STIs</u>: See “<u>Gonorrhea treatment</u>,” “<u>Genitourinary chlamydia treatment</u>,” “<u>Treatment of HSV infection</u>,” and “<u>Treatment of syphilis</u>.”

* <u>Irritant balanoposthitis</u> and allergic dermatitis

* Remove inciting trigger.

* Administer <u>hydrocortisone</u> DOSAGE until symptoms resolve. [[2]](/library/7vW4Yn0)

* Other inflammatory etiologies (e.g., <u>lichen planus</u>, <u>psoriasis</u>)

* Treatment varies by underlying etiology.

* Consult a specialist (e.g., rheumatology, dermatology).

* Suspected <u>malignancy</u>

* Consult urology.

* See “<u>Penile cancer</u>” for further management.





### Complications [[2]](/library/7vW4Yn0)




* <u>Phimosis</u>

* <u>Paraphimosis</u>

* <u>Urethral stricture</u>

* <u>Penile cancer</u>

## Phimosis

* Definition: a congenital or acquired constriction of the <u>foreskin</u> causing inability to <u>retract</u> it over the <u>glans penis</u>

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: <u>physiologic phimosis</u> occurs in ∼10% of boys at 3 years of age, but decreases to ∼1% of boys by 16 years of age [[6]](/library/AuWRFM0)

* Etiology [[6]](/library/AuWRFM0)

* Physiologic phimosis: the inability to <u>retract</u> the <u>foreskin</u> due to preputial adhesions between the glans and <u>foreskin</u> (congenital)

* Pathologic phimosis refers to the inability to <u>retract</u> the <u>foreskin</u> due to <u>distal</u> scarring caused by, e.g.:

* Recurrent episodes of <u>balanitis</u> or <u>balanoposthitis</u>

* <u>Balanitis xerotica obliterans</u>

* Redundant tissue remaining after <u>circumcision</u> [[7]](/library/2xWTDn0)[[8]](/library/fxWkDn0)

* Trauma

* Clinical features [[6]](/library/AuWRFM0)

* Inability to <u>retract</u> <u>foreskin</u>

* White fibrous ring around the preputial orifice in <u>pathologic phimosis</u>

* Symptoms of underlying etiology (e.g., <u>balanitis</u>, <u>balanitis xerotica obliterans</u>)

* Diagnostics: <u>clinical diagnosis</u>

* Treatment [[6]](/library/AuWRFM0)

* All patients: Optimize <u>foreskin hygiene</u> (e.g., cleansing with soap and water).

* <u>Physiologic phimosis</u>: Provide reassurance (mostly <u>self-limiting</u>).

* <u>Pathological phimosis</u> and <u>physiological phimosis</u> with recurrent complications (e.g., <u>paraphimosis</u>, <u>UTIs</u>): Consider <u>topical corticosteroids</u> (<u>off-label</u>).  [[9]](/library/aEWQ8M0)

* Options include <u>triamcinolone</u> DOSAGE and <u>betamethasone</u>. DOSAGE [[6]](/library/AuWRFM0)[[10]](/library/YEWn8M0)

* Duration: 4–8 weeks

* <u>Conservative treatment</u> failure: surgical management (e.g., <u>circumcision</u>)

* Complications [[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* <u>Paraphimosis</u>

* <u>Lower urinary tract obstruction</u>

* <u>Urinary tract infections</u>

* Balantitis or <u>balanoposthitis</u>
